facts.claim: UNESCO page 'Indonesian Batik' (state: Indonesia), inscribed 2009 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Re-checked live: HTTP 200, title confirmed. Reused from indonesian-wedding-traditions pack fact_01.

UNESCO's description says special batik varieties are part of celebrations of marriage and pregnancy, and batik accompanies life from baby slings to funerary cloth; the element is tagged 'Wedding'. Page re-checked live (HTTP 200); claim carried from indonesian pack fact_02 (read in full 2026-11-03).

UNESCO describes batik made by drawing dots and lines of hot wax on cotton or silk, the wax resisting dye; the craft is often passed down within families. Page re-checked live; claim carried from indonesian pack fact_03.

ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta official page 'Dhaup Ageng' (16 April 2017, re-read live 2026-11-04, HTTP 200): Dhaup Ageng is the wedding a Sultan holds for his daughter; the page states that in Javanese tradition the wedding is held by the bride's side; the ceremony has been much simplified over time while keeping the core of each step.

ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng': the sequence listed is lamaran, majang and pasang tarub, nyantri, siraman, tantingan, midodareni, akad nikah, panggih, tampa kaya, dhahar klimah, kirab, resepsi, pamitan. Useful as one documented order; not every family follows it.

ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng', lamaran: once the couple agree to marry, the groom's side shows its seriousness through a lamaran (proposal) ceremony; after it is accepted, the wedding date and the steps and people involved are set. In the royal version the Sultan then gives both a new name and title.

ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng', majang and pasang tarub: the point is to decorate the places where the ceremonies will happen and to ask that everything runs smoothly, marked with decorations and offerings; a bleketepe woven from young coconut leaf (janur) is put up on the roof; tarub (curved janur decoration) and tuwuhan (particular plants, leaves and seeds) are placed at several spots. On the palace page it is the event organisers who hang the bleketepe; the page does not say the bride's father does.
facts.conflicts: Brief expected 'put up by the bride's father'; the palace page names the event's officials for the royal wedding. Keep the father version as 'often told' unless batch sources confirm it.

facts.claim: ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng', nyantri: a welcome for the groom-to-be and his family into the palace, framed as introducing him to the royal family's customs, rules and daily life; palace relatives collect them and bring them by horse carriage to the Kasatriyan (men's quarters), where they are hosted.

Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng', siraman: the ritual bathing of both bride- and groom-to-be, meaning cleansing or purifying them outwardly and inwardly; done by the mother, the future mother-in-law and senior relatives of the bride as a blessing; bride and groom bathed at separate times and places, the bride first. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_08.)

ROYAL PRACTICE ONLY. Kraton Yogyakarta: the bride-to-be is bathed with water from seven springs mixed with flowers; that water and the relatives who bathed her then go to the groom's siraman. Do not present seven springs as universal. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_09.)

Kraton Yogyakarta: after siraman both are dressed and made up; for the bride this usually involves shaving (mengerik) the fine hairs on forehead and nape to form the outline (cengkorongan) of the paes ageng makeup. Supports ngerik in substance; 'juru paes' is not on the page. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_10.)

Kraton Yogyakarta: midodareni is held on the night before the core wedding rites, as the bride's request that the next day goes smoothly; the name comes from 'bidadari' (heavenly nymph), a hope she will look as lovely as a nymph; nymphs are believed to descend near midnight; the custom is said to follow the Jaka Tarub story, who asked the nymph Nawangwulan to come down and make up their daughter Nawangsih the night before her wedding. Nothing on the page frames it as a hen or stag night. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_11.)

ROYAL CONTEXT. Kraton Yogyakarta: akad nikah is the core rite that makes the couple husband and wife; the ijab qobul vow is spoken. In the palace it is held in Masjid Panepen, attended by men only, the Sultan himself marries off his daughter, and the groom then does sungkeman to the Sultan. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_12, sungkeman detail added.)

Kraton Yogyakarta 'Upacara Daur Hidup Masyarakat Jawa' (7 August 2017; bibliography cites a 2009 Yogyakarta provincial culture office book): marriage is one of the three key life phases with birth and death; Javanese marriage has three big stages, pre-wedding, wedding and post-wedding; the page notes traditional ceremonies are being shortened or left out for cost or practicality, while the palace still holds them in full. Re-read live 2026-11-04, HTTP 200. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_15.)

Official copy (BPK legal database, JDIH BPK) of Presidential Instruction No. 1 of 1991 on disseminating the Kompilasi Hukum Islam (KHI); re-checked live 2026-11-04, HTTP 200, title confirmed. The page holds the 2-page instruction only, not the KHI annex, so specific akad elements (wali, two witnesses, ijab kabul, mahar) are NOT confirmed from an official copy. (Re-check of indonesian pack fact_17.)

Kalurahan Girikerto (Sleman Regency village government site, culture data page 'Upacara Tradisi Daur Hidup dalam Fase pra-nikah, tahap pernikahan, dan tahap paska nikah'), read live 2026-11-04: nontoni is the first step toward marriage, a ceremony to see the prospective partner; lamaran comes second, after nontoni, once the young man accepts his parents' choice; if accepted, the bride's parents send an envoy with the answer (jawaban). Local village record (Sleman, Yogyakarta), not a statement for all Java.

Kalurahan Girikerto (Sleman) culture data page: peningsetan comes from 'singset', meaning to tie, so a peningset is 'a binder'; it is the fourth step, after the answer to the proposal is received. The page does not list the gift items.

Kalurahan Girikerto (Sleman) culture data page: putting up the tarub at the gateway of the bride-to-be's family home opens the series of ceremonies and also announces that the household is about to hold a wedding (hajatan mantu). Listed as 'Pasang tarub/Tuwuhan'.

Kalurahan Girikerto (Sleman) culture data page: nyantri means entrusting the groom-to-be to the bride's family for one to two days before the wedding; siraman is bathing the bride- or groom-to-be, meaning to cleanse oneself to become pure; adol dawet (selling dawet) follows the siraman.

Kalurahan Girikerto (Sleman) culture data page: midodareni is held between 6 pm and midnight; the bride- and groom-to-be must not sleep; it includes advice, counsel and prayers. Ijab qobul is the validation of the marriage according to the couple's religion; panggih brings bride and groom together as husband and wife after the religious and civil-registration steps; ngundhuh mantu is the final post-wedding step. The page also lists langkahan, done before the akad when a younger sibling marries before an unmarried older one.

ABSTRACT ONLY. Walisongo: Jurnal Penelitian Sosial Keagamaan 21(2) 2013, pp. 309-330, Waryunah Irmawati (IAIN Surakarta), 'Makna Simbolik Upacara Siraman Pengantin Adat Jawa', DOI 10.21580/ws.21.2.247: siraman is a Javanese ritual bathing held one day before the ijab qabul; its procedure and equipment (uborampe) are fixed (pakem) and carry symbolic meaning; the study links Javanese philosophy, culture and Islam. Abstract page read live 2026-11-04; full PDF not read.

ABSTRACT ONLY. Jurnal Sastra Indonesia (SASINDO) 11(1) 2022, Universitas Negeri Medan, Marlia, Harahap and Wuriyani, 'Makna Simbolik dalam Tradisi Peningsetan dan Pasang Tarub/Tratag dalam Pernikahan Adat Jawa', DOI 10.24114/sasindo.v11i1.36090: peningsetan is commonly called seserahan and has become a usual part of weddings in Indonesia, once not obligatory but now rooted; in the community studied, tarub/tratag is now used only at the kitchen area while the front uses wedding tents, and tarub decoration is replaced with plastic flowers; some objects and steps have been dropped as old-fashioned. Fieldwork setting (likely North Sumatra Javanese community) not confirmed from the abstract.

Widyaparwa 49(1) 2021 (peer-reviewed, Balai Bahasa DIY, Indonesian education ministry), Nardilla: a study of panyandra, the poetic narration by the master of ceremonies during panggih in the Surakarta style (Nganjuk, East Java), finding similes and metaphors of beauty, splendour and good wishes for the couple's household. Live re-check did not complete within the budget (fetch still running); claim carried from indonesian pack fact_16, read 2026-11-03. Treat as needing one re-check before publish.

Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng' (16 April 2017; re-checked live, HTTP 200): Dhaup Ageng is the ceremony a king holds when marrying off a daughter; in Javanese tradition the wedding is hosted by the bride's side. The page describes the royal procession as practised under Sri Sultan Hamengku Bawono Ka10 and says it has been simplified over time. ROYAL PRACTICE ONLY.

Kraton Yogyakarta: panggih is the meeting of the couple after they are legally married; in the royal version the groom carries 4 rolled betel leaves (gantal) and throws first, slowly, to the bride who carries 3; the bride then washes the groom's feet, followed by breaking an egg. The royal version adds pondongan (the bride lifted to shoulder height by the groom and the bride's uncle) to honour her as a daughter of the Sultan and the queen consort. The page does NOT name the sindur cloth walk, timbang/pangkon or kacar-kucur by those names. ROYAL PRACTICE; do not state counts as universal.
facts.conflicts: Royal counts 4 and 3 gantal; non-royal counts may differ.

facts.claim: Kraton Yogyakarta: after panggih come tampa kaya (the groom pours coins and various grains for the bride to receive, symbolising the husband's responsibility to provide and bring prosperity) and dhahar klimah (shared meal; the groom forms three balls of rice with side dishes and gives them to the bride to eat). ROYAL PRACTICE; these are the palace's names for what are often told as kacar-kucur and dulangan.

Kraton Yogyakarta: after the ijab qobul at the akad nikah, the groom performs sungkeman to the Sultan as a mark of respect and to ask for his blessing. This is the only sungkeman the page names, and it is ROYAL PRACTICE (the groom to the Sultan, after the akad, before panggih); the page does not describe sungkeman to both sets of parents.

Kraton Yogyakarta: after siraman the bride's fine hair on the forehead and nape is shaved (dikerik) to create the cengkorongan, the outline or pattern for the paes ageng make-up. ROYAL PRACTICE; the page does not describe Solo styles.

Kraton Yogyakarta: at the royal reception the palace dances Beksan Bedhaya Manten (Sanghaskara), six unmarried female dancers, two playing the bride and groom, symbolising the couple's journey to married life, and Beksan Lawung Ageng (12 male dancers, a soldiers' dance created by Sultan Hamengku Buwono I) are performed. The page does not name the gamelan pieces played. ROYAL PRACTICE.

UNESCO page title 'Gamelan' (Indonesia), inscribed in 2021 (16.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO says gamelan is the traditional Indonesian percussion orchestra and its instruments, 'typically performed in religious rituals, ceremonies, traditional theatre, festivals and concerts'. The text does NOT mention weddings or marriage, so per the brief the article must not say UNESCO links gamelan to weddings (it may say UNESCO lists ceremonies generally).

Widyaparwa 49(1) 2021 (peer-reviewed, Balai Bahasa DIY), Nardilla: studies panyandra, the poetic narration by the master of ceremonies during the panggih ceremony in the Surakarta style (Nganjuk, East Java), with similes and metaphors of beauty and good wishes for the couple. Carried over from the Indonesian pack (checked 2026-11-03), NOT re-fetched in this batch.

ABSTRACT ONLY: Priyatiningsih (Universitas Veteran Bangun Nusantara Sukoharjo), 'Pendidikan Karakter Melalui Tradisi Sungkeman Adat Jawa', Jurnal Sustainable 5(2), 458-462 (published 12 Feb 2023; SINTA 4), DOI 10.32923/kjmp.v5i2.3228. In the wedding rite, sungkeman teaches the child's obedience to both parents, parents-in-law and even grandparents, Javanese etiquette of honouring elders, and asking for blessing (doa restu) for a happy, lasting marriage. Qualitative descriptive study. The abstract does not fix sungkeman's place in the sequence.

SEARCH-SUMMARY ONLY (page fetch did not complete): Jogja Budaya, the Yogyakarta provincial culture office database (Dinas Kebudayaan DIY), entry 'Busana Upacara Resepsi' (12 Jan 2016) shows in the search snippet: the bride wears busana keprabon with face make-up called paes ageng lengkap, while the groom wears a kuluk (headdress). Do not expand beyond this snippet until the page is read.

Australian Embassy Indonesia 'Marriage in Indonesia' (re-checked live 2026-11-04, HTTP 200): neither DFAT nor its missions can advise on other countries' specific marriage requirements; contact the nearest Indonesian Embassy/Consulate-General or the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place; the page is a general guide only and suggests discussing further steps with a lawyer in Australia and/or Indonesia.

Embassy page: persons of any nationality may generally marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (page lists Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian); marriages may be performed by ministers of religion, Civil Registry officers (Kantor Catatan Sipil) or the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA); to be legal it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of both parties.
Embassy page, 'Couples must be of the same religion': under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974 concerning marriage, both parties must hold the same religion; if not, one party must convert.

Embassy page: an Australian marrying in Indonesia applies for a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) at the Australian Embassy Jakarta or the Consulates-General in Denpasar, Surabaya or Makassar. Jurisdiction guide (check with the Civil Registry or KUA): Embassy Jakarta covers Jakarta, West Java and Yogyakarta (among others); Consulate-General Surabaya covers East Java and Central Java; Consulate-General Bali covers Bali, NTB and NTT. CNI usually issued while you wait if documents are complete; no expiry is set but Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept CNIs issued more than 3 months prior. You cannot marry at the Embassy/Consulate-General. No fee is stated on the page.
facts.conflicts: Indonesian pack fact_105 did not record the Java jurisdiction split; new detail: Yogyakarta under Jakarta, Central Java (incl. Solo) under Surabaya.

facts.claim: Embassy page: Muslim weddings are performed by the KUA, which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah); Civil Registry registration usually not required but a Civil Registry marriage certificate is recommended if relocating. Non-Muslim marriages: lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding and register the marriage there after the ceremony for it to be legal. Documents listed: CNI, passports or KTP, birth certificates, marriage certificate, proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate (if applicable), four 4x6 cm photos; requirements vary by province. The page also notes liaising without Indonesian language skills can be difficult.

Embassy FAQ: since 1 January 1995 any marriage legally performed overseas that would have been legal had it been performed in Australia is accepted as legal under Australian law; no need to register with the Embassy; you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia; you cannot marry before a divorce decree absolute is issued.

Smartraveller Indonesia (re-checked live 2026-11-04; 'Updated: 21 October 2026', 'Still current at: 04 November 2026'): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' in Indonesia overall due to security risks (level 2); 'Reconsider your need to travel' (level 3) to Papua Pegunungan and Papua Tengah. No Java province or Bali is listed in a higher-level area. Missions: Embassy Jakarta; Consulates-General Bali, Makassar, Surabaya. Volcano list includes Mount Merapi (between Central Java and Yogyakarta) and Mount Semeru (East Java).

Smartraveller Indonesia: the revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation, adultery and sex outside marriage between a man and a woman; if married, authorities can act on a complaint from a spouse; if unmarried, on a complaint from a child or parent.
Smartraveller Indonesia local emergency contacts: fire 113; ambulance and rescue 118; medical emergencies 119; police 110 or 112 (SMS 1717).

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (updated 18/08/2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is recognised if valid where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law; not recognised where a party is already married, underage, too closely related or forced; some authorities only accept CNIs issued in their own country; talk to a lawyer to confirm validity. Carried over from the Indonesian pack (checked 2026-11-03), NOT re-fetched in this batch.

UNESCO page title 'Indonesian Batik' (re-checked live 2026-11-04), inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO: 'special varieties are incorporated into celebrations of marriage and pregnancy'; infants are carried in batik slings and the dead are shrouded in funerary batik; designs are drawn with dots and lines of hot wax that resists dye, so the artisan colours selectively; meanings come through 'the symbolic meanings of its colours and designs'. UNESCO tags the element 'Wedding'. It names no specific motif (no truntum, sido mukti).

ABSTRACT ONLY (page meta description read): Siregar et al., 'Literature Review: Batik and Wedding Customs According to Javanese Tradition', ICOMSI 2023 proceedings, Atlantis Press (2024). Batik in traditional Javanese wedding processions is interpreted as hopes and prayers made by the bride and her family for the household; batik motifs are seen as factors that bring goodness. Literature review; motif-level claims not read.

TITLE AND SEARCH SUMMARY ONLY: Pithaloka (2026), 'Kartini Princess of Java Movie Represent the Significance of Batik Truntum as A Symbolic Expression Worn by Parental Figures on the Wedding Day', Journal of Fashion Design and Textiles (DESILLES), Politeknik Kreatif Indonesia (title confirmed live, HTTP 200). A second search snippet (SMUJO journal, 'Study of Javanese philosophical values in Kliwonan batik', not opened) says the bride's and groom's parents wear truntum cloth with a sabuk kemben and sindur, symbolising hope for eternity. Supports only 'truntum is often worn by the parents' as a widely reported custom; no meaning stated as fact. Sido mukti / sido asih: NOT sourced in this batch.

insider_details.detail: Couples asking for 'the full set' should know the documented village sequence runs nontoni, lamaran, the formal answer, peningsetan, tarub, nyantri, siraman, adol dawet, midodareni, ijab, panggih and ngundhuh mantu, so pre-wedding customs can span weeks, not one weekend; ask each family which steps they keep.

Siraman is held the day before the ijab in the studied tradition and the palace bathes the bride first, then the groom elsewhere; for a destination wedding, plan two private bathing spaces and a gap in the run sheet so elders can move between them.

Midodareni runs from early evening to midnight with advice and prayers and the couple stay awake, so it is a quiet family evening, not a hen or buck's night; keep guest entertainment separate and avoid scheduling an early ceremony call the next morning without warning the families.

The tarub at the family gateway is a public signal that a wedding is coming; at a hired venue, agree early where the janur and plant decorations will go and who installs them, since many families now use tents and simplified decorations.
Palace details such as seven-spring water, a men-only akad in the palace mosque and the Sultan conducting the vow are royal practice; brief vendors and guests that ordinary family weddings differ.

The Embassy's CNI jurisdiction splits Java: a Yogyakarta wedding sits with the Embassy in Jakarta, while Solo (Central Java) and East Java sit with the Consulate-General in Surabaya, and Bali with the Consulate-General in Bali; confirm the right mission with the local Civil Registry or KUA before booking travel to collect it.

Because Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept a CNI issued more than 3 months earlier, and non-Muslim couples must lodge notice at least 10 days ahead, the CNI collection and the notice need to sit inside the same short window before the wedding date.

The Embassy says DFAT cannot advise on Indonesian requirements and both partners must hold the same recognised religion; many couples therefore marry legally in Australia and hold the Javanese rites in Java or Bali as a ceremony (offered as an option, not legal advice).

In the palace account the panggih runs gantal throw, foot washing, egg, then tampa kaya and dhahar klimah, and the groom's sungkeman to the Sultan comes straight after the akad; family weddings vary, so agree the running order with both families and whoever leads the rites before the MC script is written.

Paes ageng starts the day before: in the palace account the bride's forehead and nape hair is shaped after siraman to make the paes outline, so the make-up artist or juru paes needs time on the eve, not just the wedding morning.

Mount Merapi (between Central Java and Yogyakarta) and Mount Semeru (East Java) are on Smartraveller's volcano list; build a Plan B for guest transfers and outdoor rites and watch local alerts in the weeks before.
